newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Victorias creditors seek fast audit.
newsitem.headline: Victorias creditors seek fast audit.

text.p: A creditors committee set up to negotiate a debt moratorium with the financially-troubled Victorias Milling Co on Tuesday sought to expedite an audit of the firm's books, a bank official said.
The creditors told Victorias officials at a meeting they wanted an audit completed in one month instead of a three-month period suggested earlier.

The creditors wanted the audit completed faster so "they can make concrete proposals on how best to make a recovery plan for Victorias," Isidro Alcantara, executive vice president of PCI Bank, one of the 32 creditor banks told Reuters.
Victorias, the country's biggest sugar miller, last week reported problems over repaying debts of 4.423 billion pesos ($168 million).
Another official on the creditors committee said the banks wanted a due diligence study of the company "to determine Victorias financial debts on the books and off the books."
Most creditors at Tuesday's meeting were in favour of a plan to see if a new investor might want to take a stake in the company, the official said.
Last week, Victorias officials had said they were looking for a partner who could put in up to 2.0 billion pesos.
Alcantara, who is spokesman for the creditors committee, said the banks were confident Victorias was still financially viable and a recovery could be managed.
"Victorias is still solvent," Alcantara said, adding that the company's financial statement submitted to the Philippine Stock Exchange showed a net worth of 2.8 billion pesos as of August 1996.
Alcantara said Victorias has assured the creditors committee it has enough funds to pay interests on its debt this month.
"There is enough to update (interest payments) for everybody on March 14," he said.
Of the 4.423 billion pesos debt of Victorias, the bulk of three billion pesos carry a maturity of less than one year, Alcantara said.

Officials of the creditors committee said among the 10 to 12 banks that have collaterals on their total 1.3 to 1.4 billion receivables from Victorias are Bank of the Philippine Islands, Philippine Commercial International Bank, Metropolitan Bank and Trust Co, Security Bank Corp, Allied Banking Corp, Asia Trust, Land Bank of the Philippines and pension fund Government Service Insurance System.

"The exposure of these banks were covered by a mortgage trust indenture covering Victorias' sugar mill in Negros (in Visayas island) conservatively estimated at three billion pesos," one bank official said.
